h1: Instagram for breweries: what to post and how often
title: Instagram for Breweries: What to Post | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical posting plan for breweries on Instagram: content types, a sensible rhythm and the alcohol rules to check before you start.
teaser: Most brewery feeds look the same. Here is what to post, how often and what to leave out.
standfirst: Instagram suits beer because beer is visual and local. This guide gives a plan a small team can keep up for a year.
sections: What Instagram is good for in a brewery

It is a shop window, a noticeboard and a conversation. People use it to decide where to go this weekend, so it works best for taproom visits, new releases and events. It rarely works as a direct sales channel for beer. In many countries alcohol rules limit what you can say or sell there.

Check the platform's alcohol policy and your national advertising rules before you start. The rules differ by country. Our guide to marketing beer where alcohol ads are restricted explains how to find them.

A brewery of any size can cover its feed with three pillars.

  • The work. Brew days, tank rooms, hops arriving, a cask being filled. This is the content only you can make.
  • The place. The taproom, the regulars, the dog asleep under a table, the weekly quiz.
  • The beer. A new release, a style explained in two sentences, a pour in good light.

Rotate through them. If every post is a product shot the feed reads like a catalogue. If none is, people forget what you sell.

Consistency beats volume. Three posts a week that you can sustain are better than a daily burst that stops in March. Stories are cheaper to make, so use them for the day-to-day and keep the grid for the posts you are proud of.

Pick days when someone is actually free to shoot. A brew day gives you a week of material if you film it with that in mind. Take twenty clips and post five.

Shoot near a window. Daylight flatters beer better than most lamps. Clean the glass first, since fingerprints and foam residue show up in a photograph. Pour at a slight angle and finish with a clear head so the beer looks as it will taste.

Short video of real work does well: steam leaving a kettle, a can seamer running, a keg being rolled. Add a caption for viewers who watch with the sound off.

Write as a person, not as a press office. Say what the beer tastes like in plain terms. Do not claim health benefits and do not suggest drinking more is better. Keep the audience adult: check whether the platform lets you set an age restriction on your account and use it.

Never post anyone who looks underage in a drinking context. Ask permission before you show customers' faces.

The first mistake is posting only when a beer launches. The feed goes quiet for weeks, then shouts. The second is copying a large brewery's style with a fraction of its budget. Your advantage is that you can show the people and the process up close. The third is ignoring comments and messages. Reply within a day, even to say that the taproom closes at nine.

Reposting customers' photographs builds goodwill, but ask first. A short message is enough. Keep a note of who said yes, so that you never have to guess later.

Monday: choose the week's three posts and write the captions. Midweek: shoot whatever the brewhouse is doing anyway. Friday: post the taproom story for the weekend and put the tap list in your stories. Ten minutes on Sunday evening to reply to messages keeps the whole thing from slipping.

If you have a bar team, give one person ownership and a phone. A feed with a face behind it builds trust faster than a logo does. Keep a shared folder of the best photographs so that a quiet week never leaves you empty-handed.

Likes are a weak signal. Watch for the actions that lead to visits: saves, shares, profile visits, messages and clicks to your website. Ask new visitors how they found you. A small notebook at the till beats most dashboards.

Review monthly. Drop the format that nobody engaged with and make more of the one that people sent to friends.

Planning content across channels, setting a rhythm and reading the numbers are the parts most small teams find hard. A focused course on digital marketing for breweries covers that, with exercises on your own account.
faqs: How often should a brewery post on Instagram?
Aim for a rhythm you can keep, for example three posts a week plus stories. Steady posting matters more than volume.
Can I sell beer through Instagram?
In many countries not directly. Alcohol sale and advertising rules differ by country, so check your regulator and the platform's policy.
Only if both the law and the platform allow it where you operate. Many breweries grow first with organic posts and events.
What if I have no time for video?
Use one good photograph and a short caption. A simple post made weekly beats a polished video made rarely.
